analysis.investment_thesis: Corona Remedies is a genuinely high-quality pharma business with ~32% ROIC and accelerating margins, but at a P/E of 62x and an earnings yield of only ~2.6% (EBIT/EV), it fails the Magic Formula's "cheap" test by a wide margin. You're paying a growth-stock premium for a mid-sized specialty pharma that the formula simply cannot justify.
key_strengths: ROIC ~32% (EBIT 241 Cr / Invested Capital ~742 Cr) — top-decile business quality for Indian pharma
Revenue CAGR ~16% (884→1,196 Cr) with operating income nearly doubling in two years (128→241 Cr), showing strong operating leverage
Debt/Equity 0.10 and OCF positive all 3 years; debt spiked to 159 Cr in FY24 but has already been paid down to 86 Cr
key_risks: Earnings Yield (EBIT/EV) ≈ 2.6% — far below the 12% Magic Formula threshold; stock is ~5x too expensive for the formula to work
Large CWIP of 205 Cr (up from 65 Cr in FY23) signals heavy ongoing capex; FCF was deeply negative in FY24 (-129 Cr) and only 99 Cr in FY25 — FCF conversion is weak relative to stated profits
Small-cap Indian pharma with 69% promoter concentration; limited institutional coverage (FII 1.84%) and no disclosed market cap make position sizing and exit difficult
red_flags: Earnings Yield ~2.6% — approximately 5x below the Magic Formula's minimum attractive threshold of 12%
CWIP ballooned from 65 Cr (FY23) to 205 Cr (FY25) — capital is being deployed faster than it is earning; risk of delayed returns
Net profit jumped 65% YoY (90→149 Cr) — possible one-time or timing benefits; sustainability needs scrutiny before trusting the forward P/E of 40x
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Running the Magic Formula: EBIT of 241 Cr divided by estimated Enterprise Value (~9,336 Cr, derived from 149 Cr net profit × 62.1 P/E = ~9,253 Cr market cap + 86 Cr debt − 3 Cr cash) yields an Earnings Yield of just 2.6%. The ROIC of ~32% (consistent with the reported ROCE of 31.5%) earns an A+ on business quality, but the Magic Formula requires BOTH metrics to be high. A 2.6% earnings yield ranks in the bottom decile of any Magic Formula screen — you would need the stock to fall roughly 75% to reach the 12% threshold that makes a purchase attractive.

The business itself is doing the right things: margins are expanding (operating margin 14.5%→15.4%→20.2%), revenue growth is accelerating, and debt is being actively managed down post the FY24 capacity build-out. But the market has fully priced in the quality story at 34× EV/EBITDA. For a Greenblatt-style investor, the entry price is the whole game — a wonderful company at a terrible price is still a terrible investment. Pass, and revisit if the valuation corrects to an earnings yield above 10%.
